newsitem.title: USA: Chase says card loss rate could top 5.60 pct.
newsitem.headline: Chase says card loss rate could top 5.60 pct.

text.p: A Chase Manhattan Corp executive told an analysts' meeting Tuesday he is confident the loss rate in its credit card business will be in the upper end of the 5.25-5.60 percent range this year, although there is a possibility it could be "modestly" higher.

Donald Boudreau, head of the consumer credit businesses, was responding to a question during a three hour session in which a team of Chase executives discussed strategies and corporate goals before the Bank and Financial Analysts Association. Chase had forecast the 5.25-5.60 percent range for card losses late in 1996.

Credit card loss rates in the industry have been climbing for more than a year. The American Bankers Association reported last week that credit card delinquencies are at an all-time high industrywide.

Chase Manhattan chairman and chief executive Walter Shipley told the analysts acquisition of a branch banking system adjacent to its current geographic area is "not currently on our radar screen" although other deals are of interest
Among areas with the most appeal, he said, are equities and asset management.
Shipley said asking prices for asset management companies are high and he stressed that any deal for Chase has to make economic sense.
Peter Tobin, chief financial officer, said a $2.5 billion share repurchase program will be "substantially completed" by the end of this year.

Tobin said the company expects 1997 earnings per share growth of 15 percent, return on equity of 19 percent and revenue growth in the six to eight percent range. Longer term, the goal is double digit growth in earnings per share and an 18 to 20 percent return on equity, he said.

James Lee, head of global investment banking, said Chase has focused on growing its newer businesses where it is able to achieve revenue growth in excess of 20 percent and benefit from the leverage of the Chase brand.

Michael Hegarty, head of regional banking in the New York metropolitan area, said electronic banking is growing rapidly. He said Chase Manhattan currently has 75,000 customers doing banking via personal computer and he expects the number to grow to 250,000 by the end of 1997.

Thomas LaBrecque, president and chief operating officer, said the focus at the company since the March, 1996 merger of Chemical Banking Corp and the old Chase Manhattan has been to use technology to leverage the corporate brand and to build customer relationships.
